title_en: Fasting the Day of ʿArafah Where the Moonrises Differ
body_ar:
أنا طالب في ماليزيا ويوم عرفة عندنا يوافق يوم السادس عشر من نوفمبر بينما الحجاج سوف يقفون بعرفة يوم الخامس عشر من نوفمبر، كيف أصوم يوم عرفة ؟ أي اليوم الذي يقف فيه الحجاج وهو يوافق في ماليزيا العيد ؟

الجواب أنه يصوم اليوم التاسع من ذي الحجة على مقتضى الوطن الذي هو فيه والبلد الذي هو فيه وذلك أن أهل كل بلد عندما تختلف المطالع ويختلف التوقيت، لهم وقتهم كما أنه لا يجوز له أن يصلي بصلاة أهل مكة فكذلك لا يصوم بصيامهم، فاليوم عند أهل مكة يبدأ بوسط النهار أو آخره عند أهل ماليزيا لذلك فيوم عرفة في حقه هو ليس هو اليوم الذي يقف فيه الحجاج بل هو اليوم التاسع من ذي الحجة.
body_en:
I am a student in Malaysia, and the Day of ʿArafah with us falls on the sixteenth of November, while the pilgrims will stand at ʿArafah on the fifteenth of November. How am I to fast the Day of ʿArafah? That is, the day on which the pilgrims stand, which in Malaysia coincides with the Eid?

The answer is that he fasts the ninth day of Dhu al-Hijjah according to the reckoning of the homeland he is in and the country he is in. That is because the people of each country, when the moonrises differ and the timing differs, have their own time. Just as it is not permissible for him to pray according to the prayer of the people of Mecca, so likewise he does not fast according to their fasting. For the day, with the people of Mecca, begins at midday — or at the end of the day — for the people of Malaysia. Therefore the Day of ʿArafah in his case is not the day on which the pilgrims stand; rather it is the ninth day of Dhu al-Hijjah.

flags.context: the closing clause of the question
options: render as the source has it and flag that the question's dating does not cohere
read العيد as referring to the Saudi Eid and gloss accordingly
treat the clause as corrupt and omit it
flags.note: THE QUESTION AS PRINTED DOES NOT ADD UP. The questioner says the local Day of ʿArafah is 16 November and the pilgrims stand on 15 November, and then says that the day the pilgrims stand coincides with the Eid in Malaysia. On his own figures the local Eid would fall on 17 November, not the 15th. Either a date has been transcribed wrongly, or he means that the Saudi Eid falls on what is locally ʿArafah. The Sheikh does not address the discrepancy at all — he answers the principle. Rendered as the source has it, with nothing corrected and nothing supplied.

flags.arabic: فاليوم عند أهل مكة يبدأ بوسط النهار أو آخره عند أهل ماليزيا
flags.context: the reason the Sheikh gives for the ruling
options: the day, with the people of Mecca, begins at midday — or at the end of the day — for the people of Malaysia
the Meccan day begins in the middle or at the end of the Malaysian day
flags.note: The Arabic is compressed and the sentence is hard to construe as printed; the point is the time difference between the Hijaz and South-East Asia, which puts the start of the Meccan day part-way through the Malaysian one. Option 1 follows the Arabic word order and reads awkwardly; option 2 is clearer but takes a liberty with the syntax. A reviewer should choose. Note also that the direction of the time difference as stated does not obviously fit the geography, which may indicate a transcription problem.

flags.arabic: كما أنه لا يجوز له أن يصلي بصلاة أهل مكة فكذلك لا يصوم بصيامهم
flags.context: the analogy on which the ruling rests
options: it is not permissible for him to pray according to the prayer of the people of Mecca
he may not follow Meccan prayer times
it is not valid for him to pray at the Meccan times
flags.note: The Sheikh's reasoning is an analogy (qiyās) from prayer times to fasting, and lā yajūzu is his own word — 'it is not permissible'. He does not say the prayer would be invalid, which would be a different claim, and option 3 would make it one. Note that this is a live and much-disputed question, and the Sheikh gives one position without reporting the contrary one held by others; nothing has been added on their behalf.

This record answers a questioner writing from Malaysia, which makes it of direct relevance to the audience named in the style guide.

'Where the moonrises differ' renders ikhtilāf al-maṭāliʿ, the technical term for the divergence of the horizons at which the new moon is first visible. It is not in the glossary and should be added; the rendering here is provisional.
The Sheikh gives no scriptural evidence and no citation anywhere in this record, and none has been supplied.
